passages.title: Reading Comprehension I – Training for the New York City Marathon
passages.instructions: Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow. For items 1–7, choose the most appropriate answer for each item according to the information in the reading text. For items 8–10, choose the best contextual meaning for each highlighted word in the text.
paragraphs: Yesterday was the last day of August. During the 31 days of this month, I ran a total of 217 miles. My goal is the New York City Marathon on November 6. I have had to make some adjustments to prepare for it; so far, so good. I started a set running schedule five months ahead of time, increasing, in stages, the distance I run.

The weather in Kauai in August is wonderful, and I wasn’t rained out even once. When it did rain, it was a pleasant shower that cooled down my overheated body. Weather on the north shore of Kauai is generally good in summer, but it’s rare to have such nice weather continue for so long. Thanks to this, I was able to run as much as I wanted. I feel in good shape, so even though I’m gradually increasing the distance I run, my body hasn’t complained. These three months I’ve been able to run pain-free, with no injuries, and without feeling overly tired.

The summer heat didn’t wear me down, either. I don’t do anything in particular to keep my energy level up during the summer. I guess the only thing I do specifically is try not to drink so many cold drinks. And eat more fruits and vegetables. When it comes to food, Hawaii is the ideal place for me to live in the summer because I can easily get lots of fresh fruits – mangoes, papayas, avocados – literally right across the street. I’m not eating these, though, simply to avoid the summer heat, but because my body just naturally desires them. Being active every day makes it easier to hear that inner voice.

One other way I keep healthy is by taking a nap. I really nap a lot. Usually I get sleepy right after lunch, drop down on the sofa, and doze off. Thirty minutes later I come wide awake. As soon as I wake up, my body is active and my mind is totally clear. I’m the type of person who, once he gets sleepy, can fall sound asleep anywhere. Definitely a good talent to have if you want to stay healthy.

I have lost a few pounds, too, and my face looks more toned. It’s nice feeling to see your body going through these changes, though they certainly don’t happen as quickly as when I was young. Changes that used to take a month and a half now take three. The amount I can exercise is going down, as is the efficiency of the whole process, but what’re you going to do? I just have to accept it, and make do with what I can get. One of the realities of life. Plus, I don’t think we should judge the value of our lives by how efficient they are. The gym where I exercise has a poster that says, “Muscles are hard to get and easy to lose. Fat is easy to get and hard to lose.” A painful reality, but a reality all the same.

Now that it’s September and the race is two months away, my training is entering a period of fine-tuning. Through modulated exercise – sometimes long, sometimes short, sometimes soft, sometimes hard – I’m transitioning from quantity of exercise to quality. The point is to reach the peak of exhaustion about a month before the race, so this is a critical period. In order to make any progress, I have to listen very carefully to feedback from my body.
passages.note: Text as printed (including ‘It’s nice feeling to see …’). The highlighted (bold) words in the paper are: pleasant, ideal, efficient.

passages.title: Reading Comprehension II – The plastic problem
passages.instructions: Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow. For items 66–75, choose the most appropriate answer for each item according to the information in the reading text. For items 76–80, choose the best contextual meaning for each highlighted word in the text.
paragraphs: It is everywhere, as visible as it is vilified and criticised. From car parts to fast-food packets, plastic has covered the Earth. It has even gone beyond the Earth – when in 1969 Neil Armstrong planted an American flag, made of plastic materials, on the surface of the moon. More than 8 billion tonnes have been produced since the 1950s. Only 9 percent was recycled; 60 percent was dumped, mostly in landfills, too often in the natural world. Countless tonnes end up as permanent ocean garbage, which sunlight and salt breakdown into tiny or microscopic pieces that attract toxins or poisonous particles, which are then eaten by fishes and other creatures that become our seafood.

Although many people worry about the impact of plastic in the ecosystems and many more worry that it can impact their own health, not much is really known about these impacts. The little scientists know about plastic suggests that although it is the most noticeable pollutant, it is far from the most harmful. Using less plastic is at best a partial solution. A better answer is to collect more of it for recycling.

Plastics are made of materials that are chemically inert. This makes them less likely to be a health risk to humans compared to other pollutants such as fertilisers leaking to major water bodies. By one estimate, the environmental and social costs of plastic run to 139 billion US dollars a year, chiefly from the green-house gases, i.e. carbon, produced in its production and transportation. Fertiliser run-off or leaking causes 200 – 800 billion USD worth of damage to the ocean, compared with 13 billion USD from plastic waste thrown to oceans. On the other hand, producing alternatives to plastic is not always easy. A cotton bag must be used 131 times before it equals a plastic bag in terms of the environment polluting carbon produced in making it.

This does not mean that plastic is not a problem. But plastic ban and penalties on plastic bags may work better in poor countries which have less developed rubbish collection systems and plastic recycling facilities compared to rich countries. Prohibition makes sense in poor places like Bangladesh and Kenya that lack proper waste-management systems. It is less useful in France where rubbish collection works smoothly.

Mandating minimum recycled content in plastic containers is also a useful tool. Governments could make second-hand or recycled plastic free from value-added tax; after all, the tax has already been paid on the fresh resource material.

The wealthy Western countries alone will not solve the problem. Among the ten biggest plastic polluters all but two are in developing Asia. Together, they account for two-thirds of the plastic released into the ocean. Of these, only China could afford Western-style waste-management in the near future. Others such as Bangladesh, Vietnam or Thailand may yet be too poor for sophisticated rubbish collection. The rich world should focus its attention and resources on urging them to modernize their waste-management systems. That is the surest way to stop the plastic wave.
passages.note: Text as printed (‘sunlight and salt breakdown’, ‘plastic ban’). The highlighted (bold) words in the paper are: dumped, noticeable, damage, Prohibition, urging.

questions.stem: The writer is preparing for a marathon run in
explanation_steps: Paragraph 1: ‘My goal is the New York City Marathon on November 6.’
Kauai (an island in Hawaii) is where he is TRAINING, not where the race is. Answer: B.
tips: Separate the place where something is prepared from the place where the event happens.

similar_questions.stem: ‘I am practising in Keren every morning for the national cycling race in Asmara next month.’ The race will take place in
explanation_steps: He trains in Keren; the race is in Asmara. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following <u>is not</u> mentioned by the writer as he describes his preparation for the marathon.
explanation_steps: The summer heat (paragraph 3), the rain showers (paragraph 2), fresh fruits (paragraph 3) and taking a nap (paragraph 4) are all described.
Traffic is never mentioned. Answer: D.
tips: For a NOT question, find each option in the text and cross it out; the one you cannot find is the answer.

similar_questions.stem: A student writes about her exam preparation: she studies at night, drinks lots of water and revises with a friend. Which is NOT mentioned?
explanation_steps: Football is not mentioned. Answer: D.

questions.stem: In paragraph two the writer said, “Thanks to <u>this</u>, I was able to run as much as I wanted.” What does <u>this</u> refer to in the passage? The
explanation_steps: The sentence just before says: ‘it’s rare to have such nice weather continue for so long.’
‘this’ = that long period of nice weather on Kauai. New York is only the race venue. Answer: A.
tips: A reference word (this, it, they) usually points to the idea in the sentence immediately before it.

similar_questions.stem: ‘The bus was late again. Because of this, many students missed the first lesson.’ ‘this’ refers to
explanation_steps: The previous sentence: the bus was late. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: A pronoun such as ‘this’ refers back to the idea just mentioned.

questions.stem: In paragraph two the writer said, “I wasn’t <u>rained out</u> even once.” What does the writer mean by this?

options.A: It didn’t ever rain at all in that place.
options.B: It didn’t rain heavily enough to stop me from running.
options.C: Not even once did I run in that place.
options.D: It always rained when I was running.
options.E: I have never seen it rain in any place.

explanation_steps: To be ‘rained out’ = to have an outdoor activity stopped or cancelled because of rain.
The next sentence says ‘When it did rain, it was a pleasant shower’, so it did rain (A is wrong), but never enough to stop his running. Answer: B.
tips: Use the following sentence as a clue: ‘When it did rain …’ shows that rain fell but was light.

similar_questions.stem: ‘The football match was rained out.’ This means

options.A: the players got wet but continued
options.B: the match was stopped because of rain

explanation_steps: rained out = cancelled/stopped because of rain. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: be rained out = have an event stopped or cancelled by rain.

questions.stem: One of the following <u>is not</u> what the writer is doing to prepare for the marathon.

options.C: Lose some pounds or some weight

explanation_steps: He says he tries ‘not to drink so many cold drinks’ – the opposite of E.
He runs (217 miles in August), naps after lunch, eats fresh fruit and has lost a few pounds. Answer: E.
tips: Watch for options that reverse the text: ‘try not to drink so many cold drinks’ ≠ ‘drink many cold drinks’.

similar_questions.stem: ‘To stay healthy, I walk to work and I avoid sugary drinks.’ Which is NOT something the writer does?
explanation_steps: He avoids sugary drinks. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about the writer?

options.A: The writer is happy with the preparation he has made so far.
options.B: The writer has been preparing hard for the last three months.
options.C: The writer hears his inner voice easily as he is active daily.
options.D: All of the above statements are true.
options.E: None of the above statements is true.

explanation_steps: A: ‘so far, so good’ and ‘I feel in good shape’ – he is happy.
B: he has run pain-free ‘these three months’ while increasing the distance (217 miles in August alone).
C: ‘Being active every day makes it easier to hear that inner voice.’
All three are supported. Answer: D.
tips: Before choosing ‘All of the above’, check every single statement against the text.

similar_questions.stem: ‘I have saved money every month since January, and I am pleased with my progress.’ Which is true? A. He saves every month. B. He is pleased. C. He started in January.
explanation_steps: All three are stated. Answer: D.

questions.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer talks about changes in his body. Which of the following represents the writer’s views on these changes?

options.A: Changes to his body are due to his older age.
options.B: The amount of exercise he can do is now down.
options.C: The efficiency of his body has gone down.
options.D: The writer accepts the realities of the changes to his body.

explanation_steps: A: changes ‘don’t happen as quickly as when I was young’ – he links them to age.
B and C: ‘The amount I can exercise is going down, as is the efficiency of the whole process.’
D: ‘I just have to accept it … One of the realities of life.’ All are stated. Answer: E.
tips: A paragraph that lists several connected points often leads to ‘All of the above’ – but verify each.

similar_questions.stem: ‘As I get older, I cannot walk as far as before, and I get tired sooner, but I accept it.’ The writer’s views: A. walking distance is down. B. he tires sooner. C. he accepts it.
explanation_steps: All three are stated. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘pleasant’
explanation_steps: ‘a pleasant shower that cooled down my overheated body’ – the rain felt nice.
So ‘pleasant’ here means ‘enjoyable’. ‘peasant’ only looks similar (a farmer). Answer: B.
tips: Re-read the whole sentence in the passage and try each option in place of the word.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the underlined word: ‘We had a <u>pleasant</u> evening with our friends.’
explanation_steps: pleasant = enjoyable, nice. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘pleasant’ in this context means ‘enjoyable’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘ideal’
explanation_steps: ‘Hawaii is the ideal place for me to live in the summer because I can easily get lots of fresh fruits’ – the perfect, most suitable place.
So ‘ideal’ here means ‘perfect, the most suitable (the right thing)’. ‘full of ideas’ is a trap based on the spelling of ‘idea’. Answer: A.
tips: Re-read the whole sentence in the passage and try each option in place of the word.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the underlined word: ‘A quiet library is the <u>ideal</u> place to study.’
explanation_steps: ideal = perfect, most suitable. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘ideal’ in this context means ‘perfect, the most suitable (the right thing)’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘efficient’
explanation_steps: ‘I don’t think we should judge the value of our lives by how efficient they are’ – how well and quickly they produce results.

So ‘efficient’ here means ‘effective (producing results without waste)’. ‘useful’ is close, but efficient describes doing something well with little waste of time or effort = effective; A and D are opposites. Answer: B.
tips: Re-read the whole sentence in the passage and try each option in place of the word.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the underlined word: ‘The new machine is more <u>efficient</u>; it does the job faster and uses less fuel.’
explanation_steps: efficient = effective, no waste. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘efficient’ in this context means ‘effective (producing results without waste)’.

questions.stem: In mid-December 2019 __11__ unknown virus infected and killed a lot of people in Wuhan city in China.
explanation_steps: The virus is mentioned for the first time and is singular and countable → indefinite article.
‘unknown’ begins with a vowel sound /ʌ/ → ‘an’. Answer: C.
tips: a before a consonant SOUND, an before a vowel SOUND: an unknown virus, a university, an hour.

similar_questions.stem: Yesterday ___ unusual bird landed in our garden.
explanation_steps: First mention; ‘unusual’ starts with a vowel sound → an. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: First mention of a singular countable noun: a/an (an before a vowel sound).

questions.stem: An unknown virus infected and killed a lot of people in Wuhan city in China. __12__ virus spread very rapidly in that area and then extended out to the other parts of China.
explanation_steps: The virus has just been mentioned (second mention) → definite article. Answer: D.
tips: Second mention → the.

similar_questions.stem: I found a pen on the floor. ___ pen was red.
explanation_steps: Second mention → The. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: A noun already mentioned takes the.

questions.stem: So far the virus has infected millions of people and killed more than two million people throughout __13__ world.
explanation_steps: There is only one world → ‘the world’ (like the sun, the moon, the earth).
Answer: D.
tips: Unique things take ‘the’: the world, the sun, the sky, the internet.

similar_questions.stem: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in ___ world.
explanation_steps: Unique → the world. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: Unique nouns take the: the world, the sun.

questions.stem: Smoking causes all sorts of physical problems, __14__ millions of people continue to smoke.
explanation_steps: The two clauses contrast: smoking is harmful, yet people still smoke → contrast conjunction.
‘despite’ needs a noun, not a clause, and ‘therefore/so/because’ show cause or result. Answer: B.
tips: Ask: do the two ideas agree (and, so) or clash (but, yet, although)?

similar_questions.stem: The exam was very difficult, ___ most students passed it.
explanation_steps: Contrast between two clauses → but. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: but / yet join two contrasting clauses.

questions.stem: For instance, the main cause of lung cancer is smoking __15__ millions are suffering from this disease all over the world.
explanation_steps: The second clause adds a related fact (many people have lung cancer); there is no contrast or reason.
‘yet/however/although’ show contrast; ‘because’ would say millions suffer is the reason smoking causes cancer – illogical. Answer: E.
tips: Try reading the sentence with each conjunction – only one keeps the logic.

similar_questions.stem: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes ___ thousands of people catch it every year.
explanation_steps: Addition of a related fact → and. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: and adds a related idea.

questions.stem: __16__ the effort by health professionals to convince people to quit smoking, the number of people who smoke is not declining.
explanation_steps: The blank is followed by a noun phrase (the effort by health professionals …), not a clause, and the ideas contrast.
Contrast + noun phrase → In spite of. ‘Although’ needs a subject + verb. Answer: B.
tips: although + clause (subject + verb); in spite of / despite + noun or -ing.

similar_questions.stem: ___ the heavy rain, the match continued.
explanation_steps: Contrast + noun phrase → In spite of. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: in spite of / despite + noun phrase; although + clause.

questions.stem:
Yonas: She closely resembles you; she __17__ your sister.
Ruta: Yes, she is my twin.
explanation_steps: Yonas makes a confident deduction from evidence (she looks like you) → must + be.
‘must’ and ‘might’ alone lack the verb ‘be’; ‘has to’ is obligation; ‘used to’ is past habit. Answer: A.
tips: Deduction: must be (sure it is true), can’t be (sure it is not), might be (possible).

similar_questions.stem: The lights are on in his house; he ___ at home.
explanation_steps: Deduction + missing verb be → must be. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: must be = logical certainty from evidence.

questions.stem:
Yonas: So, if you are twins, you __18__ similar characters in several aspects.
Ruta: We are the same in many ways.
explanation_steps: Again a deduction: since you are twins, it is almost certain that you possess (have) similar characters.
must + have (= possess) → ‘you must have similar characters’. ‘need to / have to / ought to / would’ leave no main verb before ‘similar characters’. Answer: C.
tips: Here ‘have’ is the main verb (possess), not the perfect auxiliary.

similar_questions.stem: You are both from Keren, so you ___ many friends in common.
explanation_steps: Deduction + main verb have (possess). Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: must + base verb for present deduction.

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “Yesterday I __19__ your younger brother in a supermarket in your neighbourhood.”
explanation_steps: ‘Yesterday’ = finished past time → past simple.
The present perfect (have met) cannot be used with ‘yesterday’. Answer: E.
tips: yesterday / last week / ago → past simple, never present perfect.

similar_questions.stem: Last Sunday we ___ our grandparents in Mendefera.
explanation_steps: Last Sunday → past simple. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: Finished past time (yesterday) → past simple.

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “Yesterday I met your younger brother … He __20__ me of your graduation day.”
explanation_steps: The action happened at the same past time (when they met yesterday) → past simple: informed. Answer: D.
tips: Keep the tense consistent in a sequence of past events.

similar_questions.stem: I saw Aman at the market yesterday. He ___ me about the new school.
explanation_steps: Same past time → told. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Events in a finished past story → past simple.

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “Tomorrow will be your graduation day … It’s wonderful that you __21__ your first goal.”
explanation_steps: A completed achievement with a result now (she is graduating) and no finished time given → present perfect.
Subject ‘you’ → have accomplished. ‘had accomplished’ needs a past reference point; ‘accomplishes’ does not agree with ‘you’. Answer: D.
tips: Present perfect = past action + present result (congratulations, news).

similar_questions.stem: Congratulations! I hear you ___ your driving test.
explanation_steps: Recent news with present result → have passed. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Completed action with present relevance, no finished time.

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “Since I __22__ a two-day workshop, today and tomorrow, I won’t participate in person in tomorrow’s ceremony.”
explanation_steps: ‘Since’ here means ‘because’. The workshop is going on now (today and tomorrow) → present continuous.
Subject ‘I’ → am attending. ‘has attended/attends’ do not agree with ‘I’. Answer: E.
tips: ‘Since’ can mean ‘because’ – then it does NOT force the present perfect.

similar_questions.stem: Since I ___ for my exams this week, I can’t come to the party.
explanation_steps: since = because; action in progress this week → am studying. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: Action in progress around now (today and tomorrow).

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “That’s why I __23__ you this message of congratulation while I’m outside for a tea break.”
explanation_steps: ‘while I’m outside for a tea break’ = right now → present continuous: am writing.
‘writing’ alone lacks the auxiliary. Answer: D.
tips: Look at the other clause: ‘while I’m …’ shows the action is happening at this moment.

similar_questions.stem: Please be quiet; I ___ a letter to my aunt.
explanation_steps: Happening now → am writing. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Action happening at the moment of speaking/writing.

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “Tomorrow will be your graduation day … Dear friend, as you __24__ geology, there is a good chance that you will be employed by some mining companies.”
explanation_steps: Fatima has completed her geology studies (she graduates tomorrow), and that completed study is the reason for her present chance of a job → present perfect: have studied.
‘as you study geology’ (A) is also acceptable English if it simply names her subject (she is a geology student until tomorrow).
B, D and E put the study in the wrong time. Keyed answer: C (A also accepted).
tips: Past action + present result/reason → present perfect.

similar_questions.stem: As you ___ medicine for six years, you are ready to work as a doctor.
explanation_steps: Completed period with present result → have studied. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Completed action giving a present result.

questions.review_flag: Two options are defensible: C ‘have studied’ (completed studies – best fit) and A ‘study’ (names her field while still a student). Both accepted – teacher decision.

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “There are several potential employers for geology graduates, so your future __25__ very bright.”
explanation_steps: The blank needs a full verb before the adjective ‘bright’.
‘may’ and ‘will’ would need ‘be’ after them; ‘be’ alone is not a finite verb; ‘has been’ talks about the past. A present fact → is. Answer: B.
tips: A modal (may, will) must be followed by a base verb: may be, will be.

similar_questions.stem: You have worked hard, so your chance of success ___ very high.
explanation_steps: Present fact + adjective → is. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Singular subject + is + adjective.

questions.stem: Letter (December 12, 2020): “I am sure you will take the same determination from your college times to the world of work in order to __26__.”
explanation_steps: ‘in order to’ is followed by the base form of the verb → in order to succeed. Answer: E.
tips: in order to / so as to + base verb.

similar_questions.stem: She saves money every month in order to ___ a house.
explanation_steps: in order to + base verb. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: in order to + base verb.

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb: ‘If scientists develop a vaccine to treat this mysterious disease, it will be a ______ in medical science.’
explanation_steps: A breakthrough = an important new discovery or achievement after a lot of effort.
break up = end a relationship; break down = stop working; break out = start suddenly (war, disease); break into = enter by force. Answer: E.
tips: Learn the ‘break’ family together: break down, break out, break into, break up, breakthrough.

similar_questions.stem: The discovery of penicillin was a major ___ in the fight against infection.
explanation_steps: Important discovery = breakthrough. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: break through / a breakthrough = an important discovery.

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb: A: ‘Why is your class size getting larger and larger every year?’ B: ‘Because the number of students has been ______ from one year to the next.’
explanation_steps: The class is getting larger, so the number of students is increasing → go up = increase. Answer: B.
tips: go up = increase, go down = decrease, go on = continue, go out = leave / stop burning.

similar_questions.stem: Prices have been ___ every month, so life is getting expensive.
explanation_steps: Increasing → going up. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: go up = increase.

questions.stem: ‘He did not achieve his goal. If he ______ co-operatively with others, he would have succeeded.’
explanation_steps: ‘would have succeeded’ + an unreal past situation (he did not achieve his goal) → third conditional.
If-clause of the third conditional: past perfect → had worked. Answer: B.
tips: Third conditional: If + had + past participle, … would have + past participle.

similar_questions.stem: She missed the bus. If she ___ earlier, she would have caught it.
explanation_steps: Third conditional → had left. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

questions.stem: ‘The Internet is an invaluable source of information, ______?’
explanation_steps: Positive statement with ‘is’ → negative tag with ‘isn’t’ + pronoun (it). Answer: C.
tips: Tag = same auxiliary, opposite polarity, pronoun (not the noun), small letter after the comma.

similar_questions.stem: Asmara is a beautiful city, ___?
explanation_steps: is → isn’t it. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: positive statement + negative tag with the same auxiliary and a pronoun.

questions.stem: ‘______ television is the most common way of spending the evening.’
explanation_steps: The blank begins the subject of the sentence (‘___ television is …’) → a gerund (-ing form) works as a noun.
Answer: C.
tips: A verb used as the subject of a sentence → gerund (Swimming is fun) or to-infinitive, never the bare verb.

similar_questions.stem: ___ books is my favourite hobby.
explanation_steps: Gerund as subject. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Use the -ing form as the subject of a sentence.

questions.stem: Ali: ‘Where were you yesterday at mid-day? At home?’ Natan: ‘Of course. I was watching a weekly TV programme. A famous novelist and poet ______.’
explanation_steps: The action was in progress at a past moment (yesterday at mid-day, while Natan was watching) → past continuous.
The novelist and poet (ONE person with two roles – one article ‘A’) was interviewed by someone → passive, singular: was being interviewed. Answer: B.
tips: ‘A novelist and poet’ with one article = one person → singular verb; ‘a novelist and a poet’ = two people.

similar_questions.stem: When I arrived, the patient ___ by the doctor.
explanation_steps: Past in progress + passive + singular. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: was/were being + past participle.

questions.stem: ‘The teachers of the school ______ educational trips to several places recently.’
explanation_steps: ‘recently’ + an unfinished period up to now → present perfect.
Subject ‘The teachers’ is plural → have had. Answer: B.
tips: recently / lately / so far / already → present perfect.

similar_questions.stem: The students ___ three tests recently.
explanation_steps: recently + plural → have had. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: have/has + past participle; agree with the subject.

questions.stem: ‘This year’s questions are ______ the previous year’s questions.’
explanation_steps: A comparison needs a complete structure: as … as or more/less … than.
‘more’ and ‘less’ lack ‘than’, ‘as many’ lacks the second ‘as’, and ‘as much than’ mixes two structures. ‘questions’ is countable → as many as. Answer: B.
tips: Equality: as + adjective/many/much + as. Countable → as many as; uncountable → as much as.

similar_questions.stem: We have ___ books this term as last term.
explanation_steps: Complete comparison of equality with a countable noun. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: as many as (countable) / as much as (uncountable).

questions.stem: ‘She is ______ good at mathematics, but she is also good at physics.’
explanation_steps: ‘… but she is also good at physics’ → the correlative pair ‘not only … but also’.
The negatives hardly/never/seldom would contradict ‘also good’. Answer: C.
tips: not only … but (also); either … or; neither … nor; both … and.

similar_questions.stem: He is ___ a teacher but also a writer.
explanation_steps: not only … but also. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: not only … but also.

questions.stem: ‘Eritrea became independent ______ May 24 and this day is a national holiday.’
explanation_steps: Dates and days take ‘on’: on May 24, on Monday.
‘in’ is for months/years (in May, in 1993); ‘at’ for clock times. Answer: E.
tips: at + time, on + day/date, in + month/year/season.

similar_questions.stem: Our exam starts ___ June 10.
explanation_steps: Date → on. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: on + date/day; in + month/year; at + clock time.

questions.stem: A: ‘I listen daily to different English channels to improve my English fluency.’ B: ‘______.’
explanation_steps: Agreeing with a positive statement: So + auxiliary + subject.
The statement is present simple (I listen) → auxiliary ‘do’ → So do I. ‘So did I’ is past. Answer: A.
tips: So + auxiliary + I (positive); Neither + auxiliary + I (negative). Match the tense.

similar_questions.stem: A: ‘I play football every Saturday.’ B: ‘___.’
explanation_steps: Present simple → So do I. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: So + auxiliary + subject (same tense as the statement).

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences <u>is not</u> punctuated correctly?

options.A: The exam will be given in September, October and November.
options.B: My favourite subjects are three: English, geography and history.
options.C: Potatoes, onions, carrots and cabbages are vegetables.
options.D: Yemane and Sara’s office is near the new building.
options.E: Africa, the second biggest continent is endowed with resources.

explanation_steps: An appositive (the second biggest continent) in the middle of a sentence needs commas on BOTH sides: Africa, the second biggest continent, is endowed …
A and C are correct lists; B uses a colon correctly before a list; D shows joint possession (one office shared by Yemane and Sara). Answer: E.
tips: Non-essential information in the middle of a sentence is enclosed by a PAIR of commas.

similar_questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT punctuated correctly?

options.A: Asmara, the capital of Eritrea, is clean.
options.B: Asmara, the capital of Eritrea is clean.
options.C: I bought pens, pencils and books.
options.E: We need three things: time, money and patience.

explanation_steps: The appositive needs a closing comma. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: An appositive in mid-sentence is enclosed by two commas.

questions.stem: Choose the logical question for the italicized answer: ‘No, it isn’t.’

options.A: Do you know the exact location?
options.B: Is she the only daughter in the family?
options.C: Is this the only school in this area?

explanation_steps: A short answer repeats the auxiliary AND the subject pronoun of the question.
‘it isn’t’ answers an ‘Is this/it …?’ question. A → ‘I don’t’, B → ‘she isn’t’, D → ‘there aren’t’, E → ‘he isn’t’. Answer: C.
tips: Match both the auxiliary (is/does/are) and the pronoun (it/she/he/there).

similar_questions.stem: Answer: ‘Yes, they are.’ Question?
explanation_steps: are + they. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Short answers – matching question and answer
textbook_ref.rule: Short answer = Yes/No + pronoun + auxiliary from the question.

questions.stem: Choose the logical question for the italicized answer: ‘It certainly doesn’t.’

options.A: Do you think there’s an Internet Café in this street?
options.B: Are there enough computers in the Internet Café?
options.C: Does the Internet Café give service on holidays?
options.D: Do you think the computers are new?

explanation_steps: ‘It … doesn’t’ answers a ‘Does it …?’ question about a singular thing.
C: ‘Does the Internet Café give …?’ → ‘It certainly doesn’t.’ A and D would be answered ‘I don’t (think so)’, B ‘there aren’t’, E ‘it isn’t’. Answer: C.
tips: In ‘Do you think …?’ questions the short answer is about YOU: ‘I don’t think so’.

similar_questions.stem: Answer: ‘It certainly does.’ Question?

options.E: Do you think it will rain?

explanation_steps: does + it. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.topic: Short answers – matching question and answer
textbook_ref.rule: does/doesn’t answers a present simple question with does.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly used clause to join the sentences: ‘Rahwa does not like detective novels. Hawa does not like detective novels.’

options.A: Either Rahwa or Hawa likes detective novels.
options.B: Both Rahwa and Hawa like detective novels.
options.C: Neither Rahwa nor Hawa likes detective novels.
options.D: Rahwa and Hawa like neither detective nor romantic novels.
options.E: Rahwa and Hawa like either detective or romantic novels.

explanation_steps: Two negative statements about the same thing → neither … nor (with a positive verb).
D and E add ‘romantic novels’, which is not in the original. Answer: C.
tips: neither … nor = not A and not B; the verb agrees with the nearer subject (Hawa likes).

similar_questions.stem: ‘Aman can’t swim. Selam can’t swim.’

options.A: Both Aman and Selam can swim.
options.B: Neither Aman nor Selam can swim.
options.C: Either Aman or Selam can swim.
options.D: Aman can swim but Selam can’t.
options.E: Aman and Selam can swim and dive.

explanation_steps: Two negatives → neither … nor. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Joins two negative statements; positive verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly used clause to join the sentences: ‘The student is very diligent. The student won first prize.’

options.A: The student won first prize that is very diligent.
options.B: The student which is very diligent won first prize.
options.C: The student is very diligent who won first prize.
options.D: The student won first prize who is very diligent.
options.E: The student who is very diligent won first prize.

explanation_steps: A relative clause goes immediately after the noun it describes (the student).
People take ‘who’, not ‘which’. A, C and D put the clause after the wrong noun. Answer: E.
tips: who for people, which for things; place the relative clause right after its noun.

similar_questions.stem: ‘The girl is my cousin. The girl sang the song.’

options.A: The girl who sang the song is my cousin.
options.B: The girl which sang the song is my cousin.
options.C: The girl is my cousin who sang the song.
options.D: The girl sang the song who is my cousin.
options.E: Who sang the song the girl is my cousin.

explanation_steps: who + right after ‘the girl’. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: who (people) / which (things), placed right after the noun.

questions.stem: Choose the correct direct speech form of the italicized sentence: ‘The shopkeeper asked her what he could help her.’

options.A: The shopkeeper said to her, “What can I help you?”
options.B: The shopkeeper said to her, “Can I help you?”
options.C: The shopkeeper said to her, “Could I help you?”
options.D: The shopkeeper said to her, “I can help you.”
options.E: The shopkeeper said to her, “How can I help you?”

explanation_steps: Changing reported to direct speech: keep the question word, put the question back in question order, forward-shift the tense (could → can) and change the pronouns (he → I, her → you).
The reported question uses ‘what’, so the direct question is ‘What can I help you?’ (A) – but in standard English this needs ‘with’ (What can I help you with?).
E ‘How can I help you?’ is the natural direct question and matches a correct report ‘asked her how he could help her’. B and C are yes/no questions (would be reported with ‘if’); D is a statement.
Keyed A (keeps the question word); E also accepted.
tips: Reported wh-question → direct: same wh-word + auxiliary + subject + verb + ?

similar_questions.stem: ‘The teacher asked me where I lived.’ Direct speech?

options.A: The teacher said to me, “Where do you live?”
options.B: The teacher said to me, “Where did I live?”
options.C: The teacher said to me, “Do you live here?”
options.D: The teacher said to me, “You live where.”
options.E: The teacher said to me, “Where I live?”

explanation_steps: Same wh-word, question order, forward shift, you. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: The italicized sentence is ungrammatical (‘asked her what he could help her’). A keeps the paper’s ‘what’ but is itself non-standard (needs ‘with’); E ‘How can I help you?’ is the correct English question. Both accepted – teacher decision.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the italicized sentence: ‘“The match has to be cancelled due to the heavy rain,” the referee said.’

options.A: The referee said that the match must be cancelled due to the heavy rain.
options.B: He said the referee must cancel the match due to the heavy rain.
options.C: The referee said that the match had to be cancelled due to the heavy rain.
options.D: The referee said that the match should be cancelled due to the heavy rain.
options.E: He said the referee could cancel the match due to the heavy rain.

explanation_steps: Past reporting verb (said) → backshift: has to → had to; the passive (be cancelled) stays.
A and D change the modal instead of backshifting it; B and E change the speaker and make the sentence active. Answer: C.
tips: has/have to → had to; must may stay or become had to; will → would; can → could.

similar_questions.stem: “We have to leave early,” they said.

options.A: They said that they had to leave early.
options.B: They said that we have to leave early.
options.C: They said that they must leave early tomorrow.
options.D: They said we should leave early.
options.E: They said that they have left early.

explanation_steps: have to → had to; we → they. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: has to → had to after a past reporting verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the italicized sentence: ‘President Trump warned Americans, “The Mexicans and Chinese will take your jobs.”’

options.A: President Trump warned Americans that the Mexicans and Chinese would take their jobs.
options.B: President Trump warned Mexicans and Chinese that they would take their jobs.
options.C: President Trump warned Mexicans and Chinese not to take jobs.
options.D: President Trump warned Americans that the Mexicans and Chinese will take their jobs.
options.E: President Trump warned Americans that the Mexicans and Chinese will take your jobs.

explanation_steps: Keep the listener (Americans); backshift will → would; change the pronoun your → their (the Americans’ jobs).
D and E keep ‘will’ (E also keeps ‘your’); B and C change who was warned. Answer: A.
tips: Check three things: reporting verb + listener, tense backshift, pronoun change.

similar_questions.stem: The coach told the players, “You will win the cup.”

options.A: The coach told the players that they would win the cup.
options.B: The coach told the players that you will win the cup.
options.C: The coach told the players that they will win the cup.
options.D: The players told the coach that they would win.
options.E: The coach told the players to win the cup.

explanation_steps: will → would; you → they. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: will → would; your → their.

questions.stem: Choose the correct active or passive form of the italicized sentence: ‘The villagers will select a few members from among themselves.’

options.A: A few members will select the villagers from among themselves.
options.B: The villagers will be selected by a few members from among themselves.
options.C: A few members will be selected by the villagers from among themselves.
options.D: A few members will selected by the villagers from among themselves.
options.E: The villagers would be selected by a few members from among themselves.

explanation_steps: The object (a few members) becomes the subject; future simple passive = will be + past participle; the doer follows ‘by’.
A and B reverse the meaning; D omits ‘be’; E changes will to would. Answer: C.
tips: Passive with will: will be + past participle. Check that the doer and receiver are not swapped.

similar_questions.stem: Passive: ‘The school will hire two new teachers.’

options.A: Two new teachers will be hired by the school.
options.B: The school will be hired by two new teachers.
options.C: Two new teachers will hired by the school.
options.D: Two new teachers would be hired by the school.
options.E: Two new teachers are hired by the school.

explanation_steps: will be + pp, correct doer. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: will + verb → will be + past participle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct active or passive form of the italicized sentence: ‘Is the government building new oil refineries in the port city?’

options.A: Is new oil refineries being built in the port city?
options.B: In the port city the government is building new oil refineries?
options.C: Are new oil refineries being built in the port city?
options.D: Are new oil refineries built in the port city?
options.E: Are new oil refineries building in the port city?

explanation_steps: Present continuous question → present continuous passive question: Am/Is/Are + subject + being + past participle?
New subject ‘new oil refineries’ is plural → Are. A has ‘Is’ (no agreement), D loses the continuous, E is active. Answer: C.
tips: In the passive the auxiliary agrees with the NEW subject.

similar_questions.stem: Passive: ‘Are they repairing the roads?’
explanation_steps: Are + plural subject + being + pp. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: Is/Are + subject + being + past participle?

questions.stem: Choose the correct active or passive form of the italicized sentence: ‘Humans use electricity for a variety of purposes.’

options.A: Electricity was used for a variety of purposes.
options.B: Electricity is used for a variety of purposes by humans.
options.C: For a variety of purposes humans use electricity.
options.D: For a variety of purposes humans used electricity.
options.E: Humans used electricity for a variety of purposes.

explanation_steps: Present simple active (use) → present simple passive: is + past participle (used); ‘electricity’ is uncountable → is.
A, D and E change the tense; C is still active. Answer: B.
tips: Keep the tense when changing voice: present simple → am/is/are + past participle.

similar_questions.stem: Passive: ‘Farmers grow coffee in the highlands.’

options.A: Coffee is grown in the highlands by farmers.
options.B: Coffee was grown in the highlands.
options.C: In the highlands farmers grow coffee.

explanation_steps: is + pp, same tense. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: use → is/are used.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘In spite of the problems you had, you accomplished a lot.’

options.A: The problems helped you to accomplish a lot.
options.B: You had no problems and you accomplished a lot.
options.C: You had problems but you accomplished a lot.
options.D: You accomplished a lot because you had problems.
options.E: You failed to accomplish a lot because of the problems.

explanation_steps: ‘In spite of’ shows contrast: there were problems AND (unexpectedly) you achieved a lot.
That is ‘You had problems but you accomplished a lot.’ Answer: C.
tips: in spite of / despite = but; it never means ‘because’.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Despite his illness, he came to school.’

options.A: He was ill but he came to school.
options.B: He came to school because he was ill.

explanation_steps: Contrast → but. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Everyone must wear a mask, for it prevents Corona Virus transmission.’

options.A: Everyone must wear a mask to transmit Corona Virus.
options.B: Everyone must wear a mask, because it kills the virus.
options.C: Everyone must wear a mask in order to kill the virus.
options.D: Everyone must wear a mask, because it prevents Corona Virus transmission.
options.E: Everyone must wear a mask, because it transmits Corona Virus.

explanation_steps: The conjunction ‘for’ (after a comma) means ‘because’.
The reason is that masks PREVENT transmission – not that they kill the virus (B, C) or transmit it (A, E). Answer: D.
tips: ‘for’ joining two clauses = because (formal).

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘We stayed indoors, for it was raining heavily.’

options.A: We stayed indoors because it was raining heavily.
options.B: We stayed indoors so that it would rain.
options.C: It rained because we stayed indoors.
options.D: We went out in the rain.
options.E: We stayed indoors to stop the rain.

explanation_steps: for = because. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.topic: Sentence meaning – ‘for’ as a conjunction of reason

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘The student denied that he cheated in the test.’

options.A: The student tried to cheat in the test.
options.B: The student wanted to cheat in the test but he couldn’t.
options.C: The student admitted that he cheated in the test.
options.D: The student did not accept that he cheated in the test.
options.E: The student accepted that he cheated in the test.

explanation_steps: deny = say that something is not true / refuse to accept it.
C and E mean the opposite (admit/accept). Answer: D.
tips: deny ↔ admit; refuse ↔ agree.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘The driver denied breaking the speed limit.’

options.A: The driver said he did not break the speed limit.
options.B: The driver admitted breaking the speed limit.
options.C: The driver broke the speed limit twice.
options.E: The driver wanted to drive fast.

explanation_steps: deny = say it is not true. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Economic growth will have an adverse effect on the global ecosystem.’

options.A: Economic growth is very beneficial to the environment.
options.B: Economic growth won’t affect the ecosystem.
options.C: The global ecosystem will affect economic growth.
options.E: Economic growth will negatively affect the global ecosystem.

explanation_steps: adverse = harmful, negative. ‘have an adverse effect on X’ = affect X negatively.
C reverses cause and effect. Answer: E.
tips: adverse = unfavourable/harmful (do not confuse with ‘averse’ = unwilling).

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘The drought had an adverse effect on the harvest.’

options.D: The drought did not affect the harvest.

explanation_steps: adverse = harmful. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Canada is one of the world’s 20 most industrialised nations.’

options.A: Canada is the most industrialised nation in the world.
options.B: There are only 20 industrialised nations in the world.
options.C: Canada is among the 20 most industrialised nations in the world.
options.D: There are 20 industrialised nations excluding Canada.
options.E: Canada is the only industrialised nation.

explanation_steps: ‘one of the 20 most …’ = a member of the top 20 group.
It does not say Canada is first (A, E) or that only 20 industrialised countries exist (B). Answer: C.
tips: one of + the + superlative + plural noun = among the top group.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Kenya is one of Africa’s five largest tea producers.’

options.A: Kenya is among Africa’s five largest tea producers.
options.B: Kenya is Africa’s largest tea producer.
options.C: Only five African countries grow tea.
options.E: Kenya is the only tea producer.

explanation_steps: one of = among. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.topic: Sentence meaning – one of the + superlative

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘No country on this planet is as populous as China.’

options.A: China is the least populous country on this planet.
options.B: China is the most populous country on this planet.
options.C: China is the second populous country on this planet.
options.D: No country is more populous than the other.
options.E: China and India are equally populous.

explanation_steps: Negative + comparison of equality (No country … as populous as China) = China is the most populous.
Answer: B.
tips: No other X is as … as Y = Y is the most …

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘No mountain in Eritrea is as high as Emba Soira.’

options.A: Emba Soira is the highest mountain in Eritrea.
options.B: Emba Soira is the lowest mountain.
options.D: Emba Soira is the second highest.

explanation_steps: = the highest. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘With a single exception, all of the students scored 90% and above in the exam.’

options.A: Only one student scored 90% in the exam.
options.B: All the students scored above 90% in the exam.
options.C: Only one student failed the exam.
options.D: One student did not take the exam.
options.E: Only one student scored below 90% in the exam.

explanation_steps: ‘With a single exception’ = all except one. The exception is one student who did NOT score 90% or above, i.e. scored below 90%.
C is too strong (below 90% is not necessarily a fail); D is not stated. Answer: E.
tips: The exception is the opposite of the rule stated: ‘90% and above’ → ‘below 90%’.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘With one exception, every player arrived on time.’
explanation_steps: All except one arrived on time → one was late. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘They don’t know how to explain it, but I do.’

options.A: Neither of us knows how to explain it.
options.B: Only I know how to explain it.
options.C: Either of us knows how to explain it.
options.D: Neither they nor I know how to explain it.
options.E: It is difficult how to explain it.

explanation_steps: ‘but I do’ = but I know how to explain it. They don’t; I do → among us, only I know.
A and D say nobody knows. Answer: B.
tips: ‘but I do’ / ‘but she can’ = the speaker is the exception.

similar_questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘My friends can’t drive, but I can.’
explanation_steps: I am the exception. Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Doctor: Good morning, sir. Sit down, please.
Patient: __57__, doctor.
explanation_steps: The doctor offers a seat politely; the natural reply to an offer or invitation is thanks.
‘Not at all’ answers ‘thank you’; ‘Welcome’ is said by the host. Answer: C.
tips: Thank the person who offers you something; ‘Not at all / You’re welcome’ are replies TO thanks.

similar_questions.stem: A: ‘Please have a cup of tea.’ B: ‘___.’
explanation_steps: Reply to an offer → Thank you. Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Patient: I haven’t been feeling well these three days.
Doctor: __58__ is the problem?
Patient: I have had pain in the stomach.
explanation_steps: The patient has only said he feels unwell; the doctor asks for the precise problem → ‘What exactly is the problem?’
The patient answers with the details (stomach pain), confirming C. ‘Anything else is the problem?’ is ungrammatical. Answer: C.
tips: Read the reply after the gap: a detailed description answers ‘What exactly …?’

similar_questions.stem: A: ‘My car isn’t working.’ B: ‘___ is wrong with it?’ A: ‘The engine won’t start.’
explanation_steps: Asking for details → What exactly. Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Doctor: What is your __59__ like?
Patient: … I don’t feel like eating anything.
explanation_steps: The reply ‘I don’t feel like eating anything’ is about the desire for food = appetite.
Answer: D.
tips: appetite = desire to eat; ‘loss of appetite’ is a common symptom.

similar_questions.stem: Since he became ill he has lost his ___; he hardly eats anything.
explanation_steps: Desire for food = appetite. Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Doctor: What is your appetite like?
Patient: __60__. I don’t feel like eating anything.
explanation_steps: The next sentence (‘I don’t feel like eating anything’) shows his appetite is very poor.
Only ‘Not at all good’ matches. Answer: D.
tips: The sentence after the gap must agree with your choice.

similar_questions.stem: A: ‘How was the film?’ B: ‘___. I left after twenty minutes.’
explanation_steps: Leaving early → it was bad. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Doctor: And let me take your __61__ as well. Give me your wrist, please.
explanation_steps: A doctor takes the pulse at the wrist (counting heartbeats).
Weight and height are not taken at the wrist. Answer: D.
tips: Collocations: take someone’s temperature / pulse / blood pressure.

similar_questions.stem: The nurse put her fingers on my wrist to check my ___.
explanation_steps: Wrist → pulse. Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Patient: I __62__ there is nothing serious, doctor?
Doctor: No, nothing serious.
explanation_steps: The patient expresses a wish that the illness is not serious → ‘I hope there is nothing serious’.
Request/order/recommend/demand do not fit with ‘there is nothing serious’. Answer: A.
tips: I hope + clause = I want this to be true.

similar_questions.stem: I ___ you will pass your exams.
explanation_steps: Wish for a good outcome → hope. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Doctor: No, nothing serious. I’m __63__ two types of tablets. You can get them from a pharmacy.
explanation_steps: A doctor ‘prescribes’ medicine: writes an order for it, which you take to a pharmacy.
‘describing’ is a sound-alike trap. Answer: D.
tips: prescribe (medicine) vs describe (tell what something is like).

similar_questions.stem: The doctor ___ antibiotics for my infection.
explanation_steps: Doctors prescribe medicine. Answer: B.

questions.stem:
Patient: Are there any __64__ with this medication?
Doctor: You might feel a little dizzy, but that is it.
explanation_steps: The doctor answers with an unwanted effect (dizziness) → side effects.
Answer: B.
tips: side effects = unwanted effects of a medicine.

similar_questions.stem: A: ‘Are there any ___ with these tablets?’ B: ‘Some people feel sleepy.’
explanation_steps: Sleepiness is an unwanted effect. Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Patient: I am really grateful, doctor. __65__.
Doctor: Bye.
explanation_steps: The doctor replies ‘Bye’, so the patient is taking leave → Good-bye. Answer: B.
tips: The reply after the gap (Bye) mirrors the missing line.

similar_questions.stem: A: ‘Thanks for everything. ___.’ B: ‘See you!’
explanation_steps: Leave-taking. Answer: A.

questions.stem: According to the reading passage, one of the following <u>is true</u> about plastic.

options.A: About 60% of plastic produced since 1950s was thrown out in landfills.
options.B: Only 9% of plastic produced since 1950s was recycled.
options.C: More than 8 billion tonnes of plastic has been produced since the 1950s.
options.D: A large number of tonnes of plastic remain as permanent garbage in the oceans.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 1: ‘More than 8 billion tonnes have been produced since the 1950s’ (C); ‘Only 9 percent was recycled’ (B); ‘60 percent was dumped, mostly in landfills’ (A); ‘Countless tonnes end up as permanent ocean garbage’ (D).
All four are stated. Answer: E.
tips: Check every option before choosing ‘All of the above’ – here each one matches a sentence in paragraph 1.

similar_questions.stem: A text says: ‘The town produces 50 tonnes of waste a day; 10% is recycled and the rest goes to a landfill.’ Which is true? A. 50 tonnes a day. B. 10% recycled. C. Most goes to a landfill.
explanation_steps: All three are stated. Answer: D.

questions.stem: One of the following <u>is true</u> about the comparison of plastics with another pollutant, fertilizer.

options.A: Plastic is chemically more active than fertilizer.
options.B: The environmental cost of plastic and fertilizer is equal.
options.C: The health risk to humans is greater in fertilizer run-off than plastic waste.
options.D: It is hard to compare plastic and fertilizer run-off as pollutants.
options.E: There is no research to compare the health and environmental costs of the two pollutants.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 3: plastics are ‘chemically inert’, which ‘makes them less likely to be a health risk to humans compared to other pollutants such as fertilisers’.

So fertilizer run-off is the greater health risk. A is the opposite (inert = not active); B is false (200–800 billion vs 13 billion USD of ocean damage); D and E are contradicted by the figures given. Answer: C.
tips: ‘less likely to be a risk than X’ = X is the greater risk.

similar_questions.stem: A text says: ‘Wood smoke is less dangerous to health than coal smoke.’ Which is true?

options.A: Coal smoke is more dangerous to health than wood smoke.

explanation_steps: Reverse the comparison. Answer: A.

questions.stem: In paragraph four, Bangladesh and Kenya on the one hand and France on the other are mentioned. What is the reason the writer mentioned these countries?

options.B: To compare their economies and technological advancement
options.C: To compare their rubbish collection and recycling systems

explanation_steps: Bangladesh and Kenya ‘lack proper waste-management systems’; in France ‘rubbish collection works smoothly’.
The contrast is about rubbish collection/waste management (and so whether a plastic ban is useful). Answer: C.
tips: For a ‘why does the writer mention …’ question, look at what the writer says about the examples – that is the point being compared.

similar_questions.stem: A text says: ‘Solar power suits sunny Eritrea, but it is less useful in cloudy Norway.’ Why are the two countries mentioned?
explanation_steps: The point of comparison is sunshine. Answer: A.

questions.stem: According to the writer, one of the following <u>is not</u> true about the problem of plastic in the environment.

options.A: Plastic is the most noticeable polluting waste.
options.B: Plastic is the most harmful polluting waste.
options.C: Plastic is not the most harmful polluting waste.
options.D: Not much is known about the health impact of plastic.
options.E: Many people worry about the impact of plastic on the environment.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 2: ‘although it is the most noticeable pollutant, it is far from the most harmful.’
So B contradicts the writer; A, C, D and E are all stated. Answer: B.
tips: When two options are exact opposites (B and C), one of them is usually the answer.

similar_questions.stem: A text says: ‘Noise is the most common complaint in cities, but it is not the most dangerous problem.’ Which is NOT true according to the text?

options.A: Noise is the most common complaint.
options.B: Noise is the most dangerous problem.
options.C: Noise is not the most dangerous problem.

explanation_steps: The text says it is not the most dangerous. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, the writer said: “Among the ten biggest plastic polluters all but two are in developing Asia.” What does the writer mean by this?

options.A: All ten of these countries are in Asia.
options.B: None of the ten countries are in Asia.
options.C: Except for two, the remaining eight countries are in Asia.
options.D: Only two of the ten countries are in Asia.
options.E: Many of the ten countries are not in Asia.

explanation_steps: ‘all but two’ = all except two.
So 8 of the 10 are in developing Asia. D reverses the meaning. Answer: C.
tips: all but X = all except X; ‘anything but’ = not at all.

similar_questions.stem: ‘All but three students passed the test.’ This means
explanation_steps: all but = all except. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: all but two = all except two.

questions.stem: The writer discussed one of the following as a solution to the problem of plastic.

options.C: Requiring recycled content in new plastic containers
options.D: Making all recycled plastic products free from government tax

explanation_steps: Paragraph 4: ‘plastic ban and penalties on plastic bags may work better in poor countries’ (A, B).
Paragraph 5: ‘Mandating minimum recycled content in plastic containers’ (C) and making recycled plastic ‘free from value-added tax’ (D).
All four are discussed as solutions. Answer: E.
tips: ‘Discussed as a solution’ includes solutions the writer says work only in some places.

similar_questions.stem: A text suggests three ways to save water: fixing leaks, collecting rain and reusing wash water. Which does it discuss?
explanation_steps: All three. Answer: D.

questions.stem: One of the overall messages that the writer wants to convey in the passage is that

options.B: there is no real problem with plastic.
options.C: plastic is not as big a problem as other pollutants such as fertilizers.
options.D: solutions to the plastic problem have to be the same everywhere.
options.E: developed countries are not big contributors in the problem of plastic.

explanation_steps: Paragraphs 2–3: plastic is ‘the most noticeable pollutant’ but ‘far from the most harmful’; fertiliser run-off causes far more ocean damage (200–800 billion vs 13 billion USD) and a greater health risk.
A and B are contradicted (‘This does not mean that plastic is not a problem’); D is contradicted (bans suit Bangladesh and Kenya, not France).
E is only partly supported: the biggest OCEAN polluters are mostly in developing Asia, but the writer never says rich countries contribute little overall. Answer: C.
tips: An ‘overall message’ is repeated or developed across several paragraphs, not stated in one sentence only.

similar_questions.stem: A text says traffic noise is annoying but air pollution from cars is far more dangerous to health. One overall message is that

options.A: noise is a smaller problem than air pollution.
options.C: there is no problem with cars.

explanation_steps: The text ranks the problems. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: Keyed C. E (‘developed countries are not big contributors’) is partly supported by the last paragraph (eight of the ten biggest ocean polluters are in developing Asia), so some students may choose it – teacher decision whether to accept E.

questions.stem: Plastic thrown into the ocean can become a health problem because humans

options.A: like to go to the ocean for swimming.
options.B: can eat plastic parts from oceans.
options.C: can get toxins carried by tiny plastic parts through fishes from oceans.
options.D: face accidents in the ocean as plastic collections turn into mountains.
options.E: face rising sea levels due to plastic collected in oceans.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 1: sunlight and salt break ocean plastic into tiny pieces ‘that attract toxins … which are then eaten by fishes and other creatures that become our seafood’.
So humans take in the toxins through fish. B is too direct (people do not eat plastic from the ocean themselves). Answer: C.
tips: Follow the chain in the text step by step: plastic → tiny pieces → toxins → fish → seafood → humans.

similar_questions.stem: A text says pesticides wash into rivers, collect in fish, and people then eat the fish. Why are pesticides in rivers a health risk?

options.B: People eat fish that contain the pesticides.

explanation_steps: Follow the food chain. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The writer puts separate solutions for developed and developing countries for the plastic problem. Which of the following represents the writer’s views?

options.A: Developing countries need to put plastic bans.
options.B: Developing countries have to focus on rubbish collection and recycling systems.
options.C: Developed countries may not need to help developing countries.
options.D: Both developed and developing countries have to stop the use of plastic.
options.E: Developed countries need to focus on global ban of plastics.

explanation_steps: Last paragraph: the rich world should urge developing countries ‘to modernize their waste-management systems. That is the surest way to stop the plastic wave.’ → B.
However, paragraph 4 also says ‘Prohibition makes sense in poor places like Bangladesh and Kenya’, so A is also a view of the writer.
C, D and E contradict the text. Keyed B (the writer’s main recommendation); A also accepted.
tips: When two options are both supported, prefer the one the writer calls the best/surest solution – but note both.

similar_questions.stem: A text says: ‘Poor villages could start with simple rain tanks, but the surest way to end water shortages is to build proper piped systems.’ What is the writer’s main recommendation?
explanation_steps: ‘the surest way’ marks the main recommendation. Answer: A.

questions.review_flag: Two options are supported by the text: B (modernize waste-management/rubbish collection – ‘the surest way’) and A (plastic bans ‘make sense’ in poor countries, paragraph 4). Both accepted – teacher decision.

questions.stem: Which of the following might be the most appropriate title for the reading passage?
explanation_steps: The whole passage discusses plastic pollution: its scale, its real harm compared with other pollutants, and solutions for rich and poor countries.
A, B, C and E each cover only one detail. Answer: D.
tips: A good title covers the WHOLE text – reject options that match only one paragraph.

similar_questions.stem: A text covers the causes of drought, its effects on farmers and ways to prepare for it. Best title?
explanation_steps: Covers the whole text. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘damage’
explanation_steps: ‘causes 200 – 800 billion USD worth of damage to the ocean’ – actual harm done.
So ‘damage’ here means ‘harm’. danger, risk and threat are only POSSIBLE harm; benefit is the opposite. Answer: A.
tips: Replace the word in the passage sentence with each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: Meaning of ‘damage’: ‘The storm caused serious damage to the houses.’
explanation_steps: Actual harm. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘damage’ in this context means ‘harm’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘urging’
explanation_steps: ‘The rich world should focus its attention and resources on urging them to modernize their waste-management systems.’
So ‘urging’ here means ‘strongly advising / encouraging’. To urge is to strongly advise or encourage, not to force; opposing and preventing are opposites. Answer: C.
tips: Replace the word in the passage sentence with each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: Meaning of ‘urged’: ‘The doctor urged him to stop smoking.’
explanation_steps: urge = strongly advise. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘urging’ in this context means ‘strongly advising / encouraging’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘dumped’
explanation_steps: ‘60 percent was dumped, mostly in landfills’ – thrown away as rubbish.
So ‘dumped’ here means ‘thrown away’. ‘unable to hear’ is a trap (deaf / ‘dumb’); collected is the opposite. Answer: B.
tips: Replace the word in the passage sentence with each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: Meaning of ‘dumped’: ‘Someone dumped old tyres by the road.’
explanation_steps: dump = throw away. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘dumped’ in this context means ‘thrown away’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘prohibition’
explanation_steps: ‘Prohibition makes sense in poor places … that lack proper waste-management systems’ – banning plastic.
So ‘prohibition’ here means ‘not allowing (a ban)’. allowing and permission are opposites; probation only looks similar. Answer: B.
tips: Replace the word in the passage sentence with each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: Meaning of ‘prohibition’: ‘There is a prohibition on smoking in the hospital.’
explanation_steps: prohibition = ban. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘prohibition’ in this context means ‘not allowing (a ban)’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word in the text: ‘noticeable’
explanation_steps: ‘although it is the most noticeable pollutant, it is far from the most harmful’ – plastic is everywhere and easy to see (‘as visible as it is vilified’).
So ‘noticeable’ here means ‘easy to see’. B is the opposite. Answer: A.
tips: Replace the word in the passage sentence with each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning.

similar_questions.stem: Meaning of ‘noticeable’: ‘There has been a noticeable improvement in her English.’
explanation_steps: noticeable = easy to see. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘noticeable’ in this context means ‘easy to see’.

questions.stem:
PART II: PARAGRAPH WRITING. Write a meaningful and grammatically correct paragraph of about 200 words on ONE of the topics provided. You are advised to spend ONE HOUR writing your paragraph. During this time, you should prepare an outline, write and make any necessary changes to your paragraph. Write the final copy of your paragraph on the answer sheet provided; you may use the space provided below to outline and draft your paragraph. Extra paper will not be provided, so do not skip lines or write in very large margins. Check and revise your paragraph. Your paragraph will be graded on Content, Language, and Organization.
Choose one of the following topics to write your paragraph:
1. How I protect myself and my friends from the Corona Virus pandemic
2. The qualities of a best friend
questions.answer:
Write ONE paragraph on ONE topic.

Model paragraph for Topic 1 (209 words):
Since the Corona Virus pandemic reached Eritrea, I have followed several simple habits to protect myself and my friends. First of all, I wash my hands with soap and water many times a day, especially after I come back from the market or touch doors and money, because the virus often spreads from dirty hands to the mouth, nose and eyes. When there is no water, I use a hand sanitizer. Secondly, I always wear a face mask in crowded places such as buses, shops and the school compound, and I remind my friends to cover both their nose and mouth. In addition, I keep a distance of at least two metres from other people and avoid shaking hands, hugging or sharing cups and plates. Moreover, I cough or sneeze into my elbow or a tissue and throw the tissue away at once. I also try to stay healthy by eating fruit and vegetables, sleeping enough and doing exercise. Finally, if one of my friends has a fever or a dry cough, I advise him to stay at home and call the health hotline. In conclusion, these small actions are not difficult, and if all of us follow them, we can protect ourselves, our friends and our whole community.

Model paragraph for Topic 2 (202 words):
A best friend is a special person who has several important qualities. The first and most important quality is loyalty. A loyal friend stays with you in good and bad times; he does not leave you when you have problems, and he never talks about you behind your back. Secondly, a best friend is honest. He tells you the truth even when it is hard to hear, for example when you are wasting your time or making a bad decision, because he really cares about your future. In addition, a best friend is a good listener. When you are sad or worried, he listens patiently without laughing at you, keeps your secrets and gives you useful advice. Another quality is generosity: a true friend is ready to share what he has, whether it is his time, his notes before an exam or his lunch. Moreover, a best friend encourages you to become a better person; he studies with you, respects your family and keeps you away from bad habits such as smoking. Finally, a best friend accepts you as you are and forgives your mistakes. In short, loyalty, honesty, patience, generosity and respect are the qualities that make a friend the best.
